analysis.one_liner: Forces public companies to disclose climate-related financial risks, emissions, and fossil fuel holdings each year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a floor vote: it sat in the Senate Banking Committee for nearly a year and a half and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the SEC to write rules requiring every public company to report annually on how climate change threatens its business, its direct and indirect greenhouse gas emissions, its fossil fuel assets, and how it prices carbon using a government-set minimum 'social cost of carbon'. Companies developing fossil fuels would face extra reporting on reserves, methane leaks, and water use. The information would be compiled publicly on the SEC's website so investors, lenders, insurers, and the public could compare climate risk across companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors, including the tens of millions of Americans with 401(k)s and pensions, gain better information about how climate change threatens the companies they own. The public gains a transparent, standardized accounting of corporate emissions and fossil fuel exposure, and financial markets get the data needed to price climate risk and shift capital away from companies that could face sudden losses as the economy decarbonizes.

how_it_helps.text: Requires all public companies to disclose annually the physical and financial risks climate change poses to them, their emissions, and their risk-management strategies.
Directs the SEC to compile the disclosures and post them publicly on its website, updated at least yearly.
Requires companies developing fossil fuels to report reserve values under climate scenarios, methane leak detection, and freshwater withdrawals, including water taken from stressed regions.
Includes a backstop: if the SEC fails to write rules within two years, companies must follow the 2017 recommendations of the Financial Stability Board's climate-disclosure task force.

analysis.who_pays: Public companies bear new compliance costs to measure emissions, assess climate scenarios, and prepare disclosures, with the heaviest burden on fossil fuel producers and carbon-intensive sectors. Some companies would face investor pressure to move capital away from assets whose value could evaporate under climate policy.
analysis.who_pays_short: Public companies, especially fossil fuel producers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: measuring value-chain emissions and running scenario analyses is costly, and those costs could fall disproportionately on smaller public companies.

The bill hard-wires a government-set minimum 'social cost of carbon' (a 3% discount rate over 300 years) into private financial analysis, a modeling choice that significantly raises the reported cost of carbon and that critics across the political spectrum contest.
Disclosure alone does not cut emissions; it pressures capital allocation but imposes no direct limits on pollution, so its real-world climate benefit depends on investors acting on the information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core disclosure requirement is a modest, well-established ask: investors, lenders, and insurers already demand consistent climate risk data, and standardized reporting is cheap compared with the damage caused by mispricing climate risk. The most contestable design choice is mandating a specific, high social-cost-of-carbon discount rate into every company's analysis, which goes beyond transparency into prescribing an economic assumption. On balance the transparency benefits for savers and financial stability outweigh the compliance burden, though the bill would not itself reduce emissions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced; the committee held a hearing in November 2020 but never voted on it, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill with 15 Democratic cosponsors on July 10, 2019.
The Senate referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the day of introduction.
The committee held hearings on the bill on November 17, 2020, but took no further action.
The bill expired without ever reaching the Senate floor when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that would have had to disclose their emissions, fossil fuel reserves, and climate risk exposure — most visibly oil, gas, and coal producers — are better off because the bill never advanced. Investors and retirement savers are left without the standardized climate risk information the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and other covered companies

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Climate Risk Disclosure Act of 2019.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in November 2020 but never reported it to the full Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the Republican-led Senate took no action beyond a hearing.

industries.note: The bill would require detailed disclosure of fossil fuel reserves, their vulnerability to becoming stranded under climate scenarios, methane leak practices, and water use — information that would expose how much of their value depends on burning fuels the world may stop buying. Because it died, these companies avoided the disclosure requirement.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies across all sectors
industries.note: All issuers of securities would bear costs to measure and report emissions and climate risk, but standardized disclosure also protects the market's integrity; the companies most exposed to unpriced climate risk had the strongest reason to prefer the status quo.
Many large investors already demand consistent climate risk data and would gain standardized, comparable disclosures; the bill's failure leaves them relying on voluntary, inconsistent reporting.
